idea: A measured comparison drawing: the letter 'x' in Garamond, Helvetica and Futura, all set at exactly 12 point, sitting on the same baseline inside identical dotted body rectangles, with dimension lines showing how differently tall they are. Caption: 'Same size. 12 pt measures the body, not the letter.' Point size comes from the height of the old metal body, so the visible letters vary a lot. It's a quiet insider fact that designers spend years learning.

A vowel-chart trapezoid with curved arrows for the Great Vowel Shift: 'bite' /iː/ to /aɪ/, 'house' /uː/ to /aʊ/, 'meet' /eː/ to /iː/, 'boot' /oː/ to /uː/, captioned 'The Great Vowel Shift, c. 1400 to 1700. The vowels moved. The spelling stayed.' Between about 1400 and 1700 the long vowels of English shifted while spelling was settling down, which is a big part of why English spelling looks so odd. It's a smart shirt for anyone who has ever cursed English spelling.

A three-row sound-change schematic of Grimm's Law, with arrows from Latin to English: 'pater → father', 'tres → three', 'cornu → horn', labelled 'p → f   t → th   k → h' and titled 'Grimm's Law (1822)'. Jacob Grimm described how Proto-Indo-European p, t, k became f, th, h in the Germanic languages but stayed put in Latin. One clean diagram shows that 'father' and 'pater' are the same word.

An architect's floor plan of a library with ten numbered aisles labelled with the Dewey Decimal main classes, from '000 Computer science, information & general works' to '900 History & geography', titled 'Melvil Dewey, 1876: everything, in ten aisles.' Dewey published the system in 1876 and libraries still shelve by it. It's a love letter to libraries with a dry wink about how ambitious that is.

A patent-style drawing of Linn Boyd Benton's pantographic punch-cutter: a stylus tracing a large letter template while linkage arms scale the motion down to a tiny steel punch, captioned 'One drawing, every size. L. B. Benton, 1885.' Benton's machine let type foundries cut punches mechanically at any size from one large pattern, which changed how typefaces were made. It's a beautiful machine that type people rarely get to wear.

Two bracket diagrams of the same line, 'To my parents, Ayn Rand and God'. The top one groups it as a list of three, the lower one, with no serial comma, makes Rand and God the parents. Titled 'The case for the Oxford comma.' It's the classic example in the serial comma argument, and drawing it as a diagram makes the point without anyone raising their voice.

A railway track plan of the sentence 'The horse raced past the barn fell.' The words sit along the track, the reader's train takes the obvious branch at 'raced' and hits a buffer stop before 'fell', and the correct line runs off to the side. Captioned 'Garden-path sentence (Bever, 1970).' Psycholinguists use it to show how readers commit to a parse too early. It's a clever shirt about how minds read.

'Buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo buffalo buffalo Buffalo buffalo.' set on one line, with brackets and small labels under each word (city / bison / bully) showing how it parses, titled 'Grammatical. W. J. Rapaport, 1972.' The sentence really is valid English: bison from Buffalo, whom other Buffalo bison bully, themselves bully Buffalo bison. It's a puzzle for language nerds and looks great as a pattern of words.

A stemma codicum: a family tree of manuscripts coming down from a dotted circle marked 'Ω (lost)', with copies labelled A to F and small x-marks where each scribe's errors enter and get passed on, captioned 'Every copy is a mutation.' Textual scholars use this method, linked to Karl Lachmann, to work back to a lost original by tracing shared mistakes. It's evolution, written in ink.

A ruler drawn at full scale: 1 inch split into 6 picas and 72 points, with a hairline offset showing the older American printer's point, captioned '72 points to the inch. Exactly, since PostScript.' The traditional American point was about 1/72.27 inch, and desktop publishing rounded it to exactly 1/72. It's a neat, useful object for designers who care about precision.

A world map with trade routes in two line styles: overland routes carrying 'cha' (Persian chay, Russian chay, Turkish çay) and sea routes from Fujian carrying 'te' (Dutch thee, English tea, French thé), with a footnote: 'Portugal sailed to Macau, where they said chá.' Captioned 'Tea by sea. Cha by land.' Most languages' word for tea shows whether tea reached them overland or by Dutch ships from Min-speaking ports. It's a whole history of trade on a T-shirt.

A minimal map of Germany with one wavy isogloss running east to west through the town of Benrath near Düsseldorf, 'maken' written north of it and 'machen' south of it, titled 'The Benrath line.' The line marks the northern edge of the High German consonant shift, where 'k' became 'ch'. It's a map of an invisible border you can only hear.

A compass-rose diagram of reading directions, with a sample arrow path for each: left to right (Latin), right to left (Arabic, Hebrew), top to bottom in columns from right to left (traditional Chinese and Japanese), columns from left to right (Mongolian), and back-and-forth boustrophedon (early Greek). Titled 'Which way is forward?' It quietly takes apart the idea that one direction is the natural one.

A bracket diagram where the letter n jumps across the word gap, with arrows: 'a nadder → an adder', 'a napron → an apron', 'a noumpere → an umpire', and the other way, 'an ewt → a newt', 'an ekename → a nickname'. Captioned 'The n that changed sides.' These are all real cases of rebracketing in English. It's a funny, true story about how speech moves words around.

A side elevation of two bookshelves with spine lettering drawn in, and a small head with a tilt arrow beside each. One is labelled 'London / New York: top to bottom', the other 'Paris / Berlin: bottom to top'. Captioned 'Tilt accordingly.' English-language book spines usually read downward and many continental European ones upward. It's a little cultural difference every book lover has noticed.

An exploded cutaway of a papermaker's mould and deckle with every part labelled: 'laid wires', 'chain wires', 'watermark wire', 'deckle', and a sheet lifting off with its pattern of lines, captioned 'Hold it to the light.' Handmade laid paper keeps the fine marks of the mould's wires, and the loose frame gives the ragged 'deckle edge'. It shows paper as something made, not just a blank surface.

A clean line drawing of two semaphore signallers, one holding the flags for N and one for D, with their arm positions overlaid into the circle-and-lines peace symbol, captioned 'N + D. Gerald Holtom, 1958.' Holtom designed the symbol for the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament from the semaphore letters N and D. It's the most famous logo in the world, shown as a piece of writing.

The Chinese character 永 ('eternal') drawn large in brush outline, with each of its strokes numbered in order and named, titled 'The Eight Principles of Yong.' Calligraphy students have long practised 永 because it contains the eight basic strokes of Chinese writing. It's a whole curriculum in one beautiful character.

A sectioned engineering drawing of a fountain-pen nib and feed, labelling 'tines', 'slit', 'breather hole', 'feed channel' and 'air return', with small arrows showing ink flowing down as air bubbles back up, captioned 'Writing is a controlled leak.' A fountain pen works by capillary action, with air coming back in to replace each drop of ink that leaves. It's a smart, slightly cheeky shirt for pen people.

A cutaway of a wooden pencil showing the cedar halves, the glue line and the graphite-and-clay core, with a small inset map marking Borrowdale, Cumbria, captioned 'Contains no lead. Never did.' Pencils have always used graphite. After the big graphite deposit at Borrowdale was found in the 1500s, people mistook it for a kind of lead and called it 'black lead'. It's a fact most people get wrong, drawn as a neat technical plate.
